1:
Henry makes the pace of the accession the lesson. David knew himself anointed and saw his way clear, yet sent no messengers summoning allegiance on pain of death but proceeded leisurely, since he that believeth does not make haste; and though the force gathered at Ziklag might have brought him in by conquest, he that will rule with meekness will not rise with violence. He draws the rule that assurance of hope in a promise quickens endeavour rather than slackening it: if I am chosen to the crown of life it does not follow that I will do nothing, but that I will do all he directs. Wesley adds that David asked not whether he should take the kingdom, that being appointed, but only where he should enter upon it, not dishonouring the ordinance with an unnecessary question. Gill dates the enquiry to the day after the fast for Saul and Jonathan.

Why Hebron is answered three ways. Henry calls it a priest's city and a city of refuge, so that God made himself a little sanctuary there, and observes that the patriarchs' sepulchres adjoining would remind David of the ancient promise; he was not sent to Bethlehem, his own city, because that was little among the thousands of Judah. Wesley adds that it stood in the very centre of the tribe, so the whole tribe might speedily resort to it, and was the chief city now that the Jebusites held part of Jerusalem. Ellicott supplies the strategy: with most of the land in Philistine hands after the recent defeat, a strong town at the far south was peculiarly fitting for a reign to begin in.

What the anointing conferred is disputed three ways. Clarke distinguishes the two acts by their legal effect, the earlier giving a right to the kingdom and this one authority over it. Wesley puts the same point without the Latin, that the first anointing only designated the person who should be king and was no actual inauguration, which is why a third was needed when all Israel accepted him. Ellicott counts all three and pairs them with Saul's: a private anointing in token of the divine commission, recognition by one tribe, acceptance by the nation. Henry observes that Judah had often stood by itself, numbered as a distinct body in Saul's time, and acted so now, anointing him over its own house only and leaving the other tribes to please themselves; he reads the gradual rise as a figure of the Son of David, Lord of all by divine designation while we see not yet all things put under him.

The message to Jabesh-gilead is read as both piety and policy. Henry breaks it into four acts, the commendation, the prayer that God would bless them, the promise to requite them himself, and the prudent turn to gain them to his interest; of the third he remarks that good wishes are good things but too cheap where there is ability to do more. Clarke calls it highly indicative of the grandeur of David's mind, Saul having greatly injured him and still being reverenced as the anointed of God, and reaches for Saurin, who told Louis the formidable prince that he had once honoured him as his king and still reverenced him as the scourge of the Lord; he adds the political motive, that David feared the men of Jabesh would attach themselves to Saul's house in gratitude for the rescue from Nahash. Ellicott finds the Hebrew conveys no future recompense but that David, as rightful king, publicly shows them this good, and notes the old tie between a Benjamite king and the city whose four hundred virgins had been given to the surviving Benjamites. Keil and Delitzsch read the rival promotion as more than Saul's hostility continued: an open act of rebellion against the God who had rejected Saul and chosen David.
8:
Why Abner set up a rival is answered from his position. Henry offers three motives, zeal for the lineal succession, affection to his own family, or the want of any other way to keep the post of captain of the host, and draws the lesson that one man's pride may occasion great mischief, since Ishbosheth would never have set up himself. Wesley is blunter, that Abner knew his king would have only the name while he kept the power. Gill makes the kinship the hinge, Ner having been Saul's uncle and Abner his cousin. Clarke suspects envy, Abner having often been out-generalled by David. Henry sees in the rivalry a type of the Messiah's kingdom, against which the heathen rage and the rulers take counsel.

The two years assigned to Ishbosheth against David's seven and a half are the chapter's standing difficulty. Clarke canvasses four answers: two years passed before any but Judah attached itself to David; Abner effectively reigned the last five while his king kept the title; Ishbosheth was forty when he had reigned two; or Houbigant's emendation of six for two, which he declines because every ancient version and every manuscript yet collated reads two. Keil and Delitzsch reject the older solution of two years over Judah and five and a half over Israel as at variance with the plain statement of the text. Ellicott puts four or five years between Saul's death and the coronation, arguing from David's seven and a half years before all Israel acknowledged him, from the Philistine hold on the north, and from Ishbosheth's being the youngest son and now forty. Henry leaves it open, suggesting Abner declared for the house of Saul in general rather than any one person.

The proposal that the young men should play is read two ways. Henry takes it as sport in earnest, suspecting Saul had used his men to such barbarous pastimes and Abner had learnt from him to make a jest of wounds and death; fools thus make a mock at sin, and a man is unworthy the name who can throw about firebrands and ask whether he is not in sport. He faults Joab too, who had wisdom enough not to propose it and not resolution enough to refuse it, standing on a point of honour. Wesley agrees, hearing a vain-glorious and cruel man and a soldier of fortune. Clarke calls it diabolical play outright. Keil and Delitzsch read the motive the other way, that Abner proposed a single combat probably to avoid an actual civil war, and Ellicott the same, to spare bloodshed between tribes of common parentage and keep the nation from weakening before the Philistines; on Hervey's suggestion he compares the Horatii and the Curiatii in Livy, of strikingly similar circumstance and result.

The name of the place carries the memory of the twenty-four. Henry renders it the field of rocky men, strong not only in body but of unshaken constancy, who did not stir at the sight of death, and reports from Josephus that they despatched one another with mutual wounds as if by agreement. Wesley makes it the field of rock, of men who stood unmovable, each dying where he fought. Clarke gives the Targum's two renderings, the portion of the mighty and the inheritance of those who were slain, and on the catching by the head recalls Alexander making the Macedonians shave because, as he told Parmenio, there is no better hold in battle than the beard. Ellicott reports the margin's field of strong men, judges the etymology doubtful, and says most modern expositors take it for the field of sharp edges. Keil and Delitzsch note that the combat decided nothing, so a fierce general battle followed in which Abner was put to flight; Ellicott adds that the numbers were probably not large but the day a turning point.
18:
Asahel's one gift is weighed against his inexperience. Henry notes that he got the name of being light of foot as a wild roe by swift pursuing and not swift flying, judges the design brave had he been equal to it, and closes with the tag that he perished in an attempt too vast for him. Clarke supplies the ancient valuation, swiftness of foot being reckoned a great accomplishment among the heroes, Homer giving Achilles the epithet of swift-footed no fewer than thirty times in the Ilias, and Roman soldiers being taught both to run swiftly and to swim well. Gill is less admiring, having him trust his swiftness without considering that the race is not always to the swift, and that he was a raw young man matched against a veteran. Henry draws the rule that in all contests it is wisdom to compare our own strength with our adversaries' and to take heed of being partial to ourselves in the comparison.

Abner's reluctance to kill him is explained four ways, one of them remarkable. Keil and Delitzsch find he did not want to put the young hero to death out of regard for Joab and their former friendship. Ellicott allows the extreme youth may have told but makes the chief cause a dread of Joab's vengeance, and Clarke the same, until Asahel's obstinacy left him the choice of killing or being killed. Gill adds a respect for Asahel himself alongside the fear of his brother. Henry takes it further: Abner's care how he should lift up his face to Joab gives cause to suspect that he really believed David would have the kingdom at last, by the divine designation, and that in opposing him he was acting against his own conscience. Wesley hears in the offer an old and experienced captain telling the young man to try his skill on some raw soldier and take his arms from him.

What exactly the weapon did is disputed. Henry reads a back stroke with the hinder end of the spear, from which Asahel feared no danger, a pass he had not learned to guard against and which Abner had perhaps used before. Keil and Delitzsch say the lower end appears to have been pointed, and put the wound in the abdomen with the spear coming out behind. Ellicott agrees the spears were sharpened at the hinder end for sticking into the ground, and adds that the fifth rib, here and wherever else the phrase occurs, should be rendered abdomen. Clarke reads it differently, taking the turning about to pierce him as what our version calls the hinder end, so that Abner ran the spear through with the point; and he notes the stroke cost Abner his own life in the next chapter. Clarke and Wesley both record the trophy motive, that Asahel coveted Abner's armour as ancient heroes did.

The death breaks off the battle. Henry observes that the fall was not only Abner's security but put a full stop to the pursuit and gave him time to rally, since all who came to the place stood still, only Joab and Abishai being exasperated rather than disheartened. He takes two lessons from the manner of it, that death often comes by ways we least suspect, since who would fear the butt end of a spear, and that we are betrayed by the accomplishments we are proud of, his swiftness forwarding his fate so that with it he ran upon his death instead of from it; Wesley repeats the second almost word for word. On the ground covered, Keil and Delitzsch say nothing further is known of the places named, while Ellicott conjectures from the way of the wilderness of Gibeon that the hill lay not far from that town, so the pursuit was not a long one, the sun going down as they reached it.
25:
Abner's plea is read as self-interest confessing itself. Henry points out that the man most forward to fight was the first to have enough of it, and that he who made a jest of bloodshed is shocked at it on the losing side; in the morning it was but playing with the sword, and now the question is whether the sword shall devour for ever, though it had devoured one day only and seemed long because it went against him. He draws two rules from it, that men use reason readily when it makes for them who would not use it if it made against them, and that the issue of things alters men's minds, since what looked pleasant in the morning looked dismal at night. He adds that every sin is bitterness in the latter end, biting like a serpent those on whom it fawned.

Others read the appeal more charitably. Keil and Delitzsch take it at face value, a warning of the consequences of a desperate struggle and a call to end it. Ellicott wonders whether Abner was already weighing the expediency of transferring his allegiance to the house of David, having seen enough of Ishbosheth to know the tribes could never be united under him; at the least his sense of the effects of civil war was quickened by his own defeat and present danger. Clarke marks the day as the commencement of the civil wars and properly of the division of the two kingdoms, through which both nations were deluged with blood.

Joab's answer admits of two constructions, and Ellicott sets them out. Either Joab throws the whole blame on Abner, since without the combat of champions the two peoples would have parted peaceably at Gibeon, or, as he thinks more probable, Joab means he had intended to press the pursuit only until morning and is content to stop now that Abner sues for it. Keil and Delitzsch take the first, holding that Joab threw all the blame on the man who instigated the single combat, which decided nothing and was so bloody that the two armies felt obliged to fight it out. Clarke and Wesley take the first too, Wesley adding that all might have ended in an amicable agreement that morning had Abner so pleased. Henry agrees and puts an aphorism to it, that those forward to make mischief are commonly the first to complain of it; yet he praises what followed, since Joab, pitying the mistake of his adversaries and scorning to make an army of Israelites pay for their commander's folly, stopped the pursuit by sound of trumpet, it being good husbandry to be sparing of blood.

The reckoning afterwards is worked out closely. Keil and Delitzsch account for nineteen dead against three hundred and sixty by the quality of the troops, Joab's being the well-tried men who had gathered round David long before, Abner's the remnants of the army beaten upon Gilboa and weakened further by their attempts on the land the Philistines held. Ellicott allows that and adds the advantage bow and spear give the pursuer, while leaving it uncertain whether the figures include the twenty-four champions. On the route home Keil and Delitzsch argue that Bithron must be a district and not a city, since the text says all of it, and reject both the old identification with Bethhoron in Aquila and the Vulgate and the modern conjecture of Bethharam. Ellicott times the march, holding that Joab got no farther than Gibeon that evening and that the night was perhaps chosen for the thirteen miles from Bethlehem to avoid the heat. Henry and Wesley both close on the funeral, that distinctions are made between the dust of some and of others, but in the resurrection none will be made except between the godly and the ungodly, and that one remains for ever.
